clue.text: Crew in a fight, possibly giving employment in the Blitz

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the words before it are to be reordered

parts.note: all twelve letters of these three words used as raw material

explanation.surface: A sailor caught up in a brawl somehow finds himself a wartime job.
explanation.walkthrough: The Blitz was the German bombing of British cities in 1940-41; civilians took turns on rooftops watching for incendiary bombs.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire-watching was a civilian wartime duty, spotting incendiary bombs during the bombing raids on London.

clue.text: Most suitable match for survivors?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: superlative of fit, best adapted
second meaning: those who survive natural selection, as in Darwin's survival of the phrase's winners

explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to 'survival of the fittest': the ones who survive are by definition the best matched to their surroundings.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of fit means best adapted, and evolutionary theory says the best adapted organisms are the ones that survive.

clue.text: Poet having the edge when it comes to speed of transmission

parts.note: a rim is an edge or border
the baud is a unit of signalling speed in data transmission

explanation.surface: A poet with an advantage when it comes to sending messages quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the edge' reads as having an advantage, but the edge is a literal border.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Rimbaud was a nineteenth-century French Symbolist writer of verse, author of Une Saison en enfer.

clue.text: A dog that's large, beginning to fill house, gets turned out

indicators.note: out here means on the outside, so the turned word wraps round the rest

parts.note: wound is the past tense of wind, to turn
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of fill
HO is the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A big dog gets thrown out after starting to take over the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' reads as evicted, but the word means wound round, with out marking that it goes on the outside. 'That's large' is a hint the definition shares with the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolfhound, such as the Irish breed, is a very tall hunting hound, once used to chase wolves.

clue.text: In Versailles you stick up for the royal family

parts.note: tu is the French for you, and Versailles is in France

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a rod is a stick

explanation.surface: Someone in France defends a royal dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up for' looks like the phrase meaning defend; up actually turns the stick over.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudors were the English ruling dynasty from Henry VII in 1485 to the death of Elizabeth I.

clue.text: Writing concealed by heart-rending creature in a cage

indicators.note: what is concealed by something is hidden inside it
rending tears something apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: used as written before being torn up
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: A sad piece of writing about a poor animal shut in a cage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart-rending' looks like one word meaning distressing; split, it is the fodder and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamsters are small rodents commonly kept as household pets inside wire enclosures.

clue.text: Like a professor in the cinema, but more so? Teachers bank on it

definitions.text: Like a professor in the cinema, but more so?

parts.note: NUT was the National Union of Teachers, a British trade union
a bank, as of seats or oars, is a row or tier

explanation.surface: Teachers are relying on something, following a remark about a film professor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nutty Professor is a film comedy; 'but more so' asks for the comparative of nutty.
explanation.definitionFit: The film title The Nutty Professor gives the adjective, and going beyond it calls for its comparative form.

clue.text: What resurrectionists do about Queen Margaret's last poet

indicators.note: about means around, so the opening phrase goes round the others

parts.note: resurrectionists were nineteenth-century body snatchers who dug up corpses for anatomists
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher for the Queen

indicators.note: the last of a name is its final letter alone

parts.note: the final letter of Margaret

explanation.surface: Body snatchers, a queen and a woman named Margaret oddly gathered round a dead poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Robbing graves is exactly what body snatchers did, so the phrase splits neatly round the inserted pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Graves was an English writer of verse and the novel I, Claudius, and a First World War memoirist.

clue.text: Tiny lad cast in stone? That's the best one can hope for

definitions.text: the best one can hope for

indicators.note: something cast in a material is set inside it

parts.note: an opal is a gemstone
Tiny Tim is the sickly boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol

explanation.surface: A statue of a little boy carved in stone is the ideal outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimal describes the most favourable possible outcome, the ideal result under the circumstances.

clue.text: Goddess using force to feed animals

indicators.note: feeding puts something into a mouth, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: deer are animals
the Met is London's Metropolitan Police force

explanation.surface: A goddess forcibly feeding the beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met, short for the Metropolitan Police, is the force that polices London.
explanation.definitionFit: Demeter is the Greek deity of the harvest and grain, mother of Persephone.

clue.text: Getting together again — like outside, like inside

indicators.note: outside says the first piece wraps round the second
inside says the second piece sits within the first

parts.note: resembling means like, similar to
as also means like, in comparisons

explanation.surface: Rejoining a group whose members look alike from every angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word is used for two different synonyms, one long and one short.
explanation.definitionFit: Reassembling means gathering once more, as people meet up after a break.

clue.text: English woods producing fiddlesticks!

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
two trees: the yew and the ash

explanation.surface: English forests give rise to an exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddlesticks' suggests wooden bows from the woods, but it is the exclamation meaning nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive interjections meaning nonsense or rubbish.

clue.text: A stein brought round after the last of the summer wine

indicators.note: after says the first piece follows the second
the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of summer

indicators.note: bringing something round turns it about, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: used as written before being reordered

explanation.surface: A beer mug passed round at the end of summer, echoing the TV comedy Last of the Summer Wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white or rosé drink flavoured with pine resin.

clue.text: To take a king away, duke must also be carried

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: taking something away removes it from the word

parts.note: taken as written, before letters are removed
a as written, and K, the chess abbreviation for king
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: If the king is removed, the duke too must be borne away.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing A and K from TAKE leaves TE; TO + TE + D gives TOTED.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote something is to lug or haul it, so toted means hauled or borne.

clue.text: Ready for war in pits?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: soldiers armed and enlisted
second meaning: armpits, the hollows beneath the shoulders

explanation.walkthrough: Pits suggests trenches or mines in a war picture, but it means armpits.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops bearing weapons are said to be under arms; the hollows of the body beneath the shoulders are armpits.

clue.text: Verdi's fourth opera about an upstanding sculptor

indicators.note: the fourth of a word is the letter in fourth position

parts.note: the fourth letter of Verdi

indicators.note: about means around, so the opera goes round the other piece

parts.note: Otello is Verdi's opera based on Othello

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Verdi opera about an honourable sculptor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Verdi's fourth opera' looks like a request for an opera title; fourth picks a letter, and Otello is a different Verdi work.
explanation.definitionFit: Donatello was the Florentine Renaissance artist famous for his bronze David.

clue.text: Conductor and professor wouldn''t stop talking

parts.note: Sir Simon Rattle, the British orchestral conductor
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A conductor and an academic who chattered on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle on is an idiom for chattering at length without pause.

clue.text: Spooner's low bit is over the top

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the starts of words, so the opening sounds of the two words trade places

parts.note: a cow's low is a moo, and a bit is a touch

explanation.surface: A vulgar remark is excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: MOO TOUCH with the first sounds swapped becomes TOO MUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the top is an idiom for excessive, beyond what is reasonable.

clue.text: Pressurised nitrogen stored under shed

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece stored under another sits below it, so it comes after

parts.note: a lean-to is a shed built against a wall
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: Compressed gas kept beneath an outbuilding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressurised nitrogen' reads as one phrase; pressurised is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean on someone is an idiom for putting pressure on them to comply.

clue.text: A light neither fore nor aft

parts.note: taken as written
a beam is a ray of light

explanation.surface: A lamp placed amidships on a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Abeam is a nautical term meaning at right angles to a ship's keel, off its side rather than ahead or astern.

clue.text: A paper product in dispute

parts.note: taken as written
tissue is a soft paper product

explanation.surface: An argument over a disposable paper hanky.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter at issue is one being debated or contested.

clue.text: No democrat wants one's title changed

indicators.note: something changed is altered, so these letters take a new order

parts.note: one is I, so one's (one is) gives I and S
taken as written

explanation.surface: An anti-democrat wishes to have his rank altered.
explanation.definitionFit: A snob who favours rule by a select few is the opposite of someone committed to popular government.

clue.text: Profane love at one remove

indicators.note: a remove is a shift of position, so the letters are moved about

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Irreverent love conducted at a distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At one remove' is the idiom for indirectly; here remove is a noun for a move.
explanation.definitionFit: Profane as a verb means to desecrate or treat something sacred with disrespect.

clue.text: Provide for party in various ways, as does the sparrow or the crow

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: three compass points: east, north and west
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Throwing a party with assorted touches, like birds do.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail is a second joke: sparrow and crow both END in OW, so the answer split as END OW describes them too.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow someone is to give them money or property that supports them, to make provision for them.

clue.text: Four or six in rehearsal? That's not important

indicators.note: in places the number inside the other word

parts.note: a trial run is a rehearsal
Roman numerals: IV is four and VI six, and either reads the same in the grid

explanation.surface: Whether four or six people turn up to practice doesn't matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers IV or VI; both spell the same letters once inside, so either works.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial means slight, petty, of little significance.

clue.text: Engaged in daring activities, like bonsai?

explanation.walkthrough: Bonsai are miniature trees kept small by pruning roots and branches.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing stunts in the past tense, and having growth checked, are two senses of the same word.

clue.text: Like Sappho, born in an isle abroad

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
abroad means scattered widely, so the letters are dispersed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written before being reordered
B is the abbreviation for born

explanation.surface: Sappho was born on a foreign island.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappho came from Lesbos, so the surface is apt as well as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sappho, the Greek poet of Lesbos, wrote love verse to women; the adjective derives from her island.

clue.text: Trees oft hewn in Hants?

indicators.note: the question mark warns that the words are not to be read at face value but rearranged

parts.note: all twelve letters reused as raw material

explanation.surface: Woodland often felled in Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Hants is the abbreviation for Hampshire, the southern English county; the whole clue describes the answer as well as spelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: This large ancient woodland in Hampshire was a royal hunting forest where timber has long been cut.
